It's a multi-faceted approach. Situational awareness, going with your gut and avoiding bad situations altogether if possible. I'm not talking about living in fear/never leaving the house, just using common sense. Examples, parking around people in well lit areas at night. Being aware that someone seems suspicious and either avoiding them, or passively showing that you are aware of your surroundings and their presence.

A big piece of the puzzle is recognizing a threat and putting your response into effect. A common problem I see is with so many people's attitudes. Many seem to think, "I have a gun and I'll shoot a mofo to defend myself." The line of using deadly force isn't always black and white.

Assuming we're all on the same page, being confronted by an active shooter or a mugger/car jacker/home invader is fairly cut and dry. De-escalation comes into play in normal everyday life. Pissed off people who are road raging, angry customers in a public business or venue are places where it comes into play. By no means am I saying turn into a tail tucking beta personality. Also, being overly alpha type is hugely counterproductive. Here we're talking about encountering a scenario where violence has not yet occurred but is imminent. There may have been a brief physical scuffle but no physical violence is taking place. That said, the person may be physically aggressive.

First and foremost... Recognize the situation taking place.

  1. Evaluate and read the person. It only takes a moment. Is the person simply angry? Is the person irrational? If so, does it seem to be only because they're angry and overreacting? Just as important, do they appear to be under the influence of a substance?

  2. Engage the person in dialogue. Ask why they're upset. Be assertive, NOT aggressive in your words. While engaged, once you know what has them so riled up, express empathy for them. Even if you think they're iff their rocker for being enraged over something that may be petty to you, convey some genuine understanding, as human beings can be triggered by somehting small when there's a larger problem in their life.

  3. While talking to the person, ask if there's anything else upsetting them, this can help find the root cause of their anger. You'll have to be flexible based on thr specific nature of the situation, as soon as possible, try to smoothly transition to a new topic. Tying in the current matter with something similar ot related, i.e. "you experienced the same/similar this one time". Transitioning allows you to gently close the door on what has them angry and gets them thinking about something different. Slam the door shut and you can further enrage a person who now thinks you're another jackass who doesn't care.

  4. Suggest an alternative course of action, offer a solution. It is critical to offer and suggest. Do NOT tell them what to do. You're trying to de-escalate and diffuse. Giving instructions/orders can reignite the problem. Depending on the person, it is often helpful to remind them of the bigger picture. "Hey man, I know you're pissed. I understand. I empathize with you. But, if you want this fixed, there may be a better way. If you get to fired up and get physical think about the consequences." This is a good point to reiterate and again offer potential solutions.

Keeping a person engaged may stop physical actions. At least other bystanders will have a chance to vacate. Ideally, some will follow your lead and assist.
